findings.title: PEM-format private key block
findings.description: Pattern matching rule 'pem-private-key' (PEM-format private key block) was found in this file. (Extracted from embedded strings inside a PE binary.)
findings.remediation: Remove hardcoded credentials/secrets from source and configuration files. Use a secrets manager (Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault) or environment variables injected at runtime, and rotate the exposed credential immediately.
findings.poc:
1. Extract printable strings from the binary directly to confirm independently:
   Windows (Sysinternals strings.exe):
     strings64.exe -n 6 "C:\Users\ankes\Downloads\Securis360\Clients\STL-Ajax\neox-one window app\Release\libmpv-2.dll" | findstr /i "-----BEG"
   Linux:
     strings -n 6 "C:\Users\ankes\Downloads\Securis360\Clients\STL-Ajax\neox-one window app\Release\libmpv-2.dll" | grep -i '-----BEG'

2. Open libmpv-2.dll in a PE viewer (CFF Explorer, Detect It Easy, or IDA/Ghidra) and locate the string in the resource/data section to confirm it is not dead code or a leftover debug string.

3. If confirmed live, treat this the same as a config-file secret: rotate the credential and remove it from the compiled binary — hardcoded strings in compiled code are trivially recoverable with basic reverse-engineering tools regardless of packing.

4. Evidence: -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----

findings.title: Dynamic library loading without safe search-order controls
findings.evidence: Imports LoadLibrary(A/W) but no SetDllDirectory/SetDefaultDllDirectories/AddDllDirectory call detected
findings.description: This binary dynamically loads libraries at runtime but shows no evidence of restricting the DLL search order (e.g. via SetDllDirectory or SetDefaultDllDirectories). By default, Windows' DLL search order can include the current working directory and other attacker-influenceable locations ahead of System32, depending on how the DLL is loaded and OS version/mitigations.
findings.remediation: Call SetDefaultDllDirectories(LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32) early in the application, use fully-qualified paths when loading DLLs, and avoid loading libraries by bare name from an attacker-writable working directory.

findings.description: Binaries within this application are signed by more than one distinct publisher/subject. This can be legitimate (bundled third-party redistributables) but can also be a supply-chain inconsistency signal — e.g. a component replaced or injected after the original release build.
findings.remediation: Confirm each distinct publisher is an expected, legitimate dependency. Investigate any binary signed by an unexpected or unfamiliar publisher.
findings.poc:
1. List every signed binary and its signer directly:
     Windows (PowerShell), for each file in the app directory:
       Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Include *.exe,*.dll | ForEach-Object { Get-AuthenticodeSignature $_.FullName } | Select Path, @{N='Signer';E={$_.SignerCertificate.Subject}}

2. Cross-reference the resulting publisher list against: Microsoft Corporation: 1 file(s); Microsoft Code Signing PCA 2010: 1 file(s); DigiCert Trusted G4 Code Signing RSA4096 SHA384 2021 CA1: 4 file(s); Google LLC: 4 file(s)

3. For each unexpected publisher, research whether it corresponds to a known, legitimate third-party dependency (e.g. a bundled runtime, installer framework, or licensed component) versus an unexplained addition. Check the file's build/modification timestamp against the rest of the release to see if it was added out-of-band from the main build.

4. If a component with an unfamiliar publisher can't be attributed to a known legitimate dependency, treat it as requiring escalation and manual deep-dive (static/behavioral analysis of that specific binary).
